claims.text: Premelting and melting behavior in high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles is governed primarily by configurational-entropy-induced broadening of two-phase fields rather than by size-related surface effects.
Increasing compositional variety increases configurational entropy.
Composition changes that increase configurational entropy systematically shift the onset of premelting.
Composition changes that increase configurational entropy alter the melting-transition profile.
Higher configurational entropy broadens the two-phase fields in the alloy phase diagram.
Broadening of the two-phase field lowers the energy barrier for phase transitions.
The lowered phase-transition barrier shifts the onset temperature of premelting.
The lowered phase-transition barrier alters melting kinetics.
The proposed configurational-entropy effect is more pronounced in multicomponent systems than in binary or ternary alloys.
Higher-configurational-entropy nanoparticles will have a lower premelting-onset temperature than binary or ternary baseline nanoparticles.
Higher-configurational-entropy nanoparticles will have a broader melting transition than binary or ternary baseline nanoparticles.
Binary or ternary alloy nanoparticles have narrower two-phase fields than the proposed high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
The hypothesis applies above a critical particle size where configurational-entropy effects dominate surface-energy contributions.
Surface effects are expected to predominate in very small nanoparticles below 10 nm.
Holding nanoparticle size and shape constant while varying composition is intended to distinguish configurational-entropy effects from size-related surface effects.
A lack of correlation between configurational entropy and either premelting onset or melting-transition width would falsify the hypothesis.
